evaluation.positioning_hook: A high-school English teacher who moonlights as a sadistic nightclub attacker must keep her marriage, her student confidant, and a citywide manhunt from colliding before Halloween exposes everything.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The hook is immediate and the Halloween countdown gives it a clean commercial engine, but the material is niche in its tonal extremity and character psychology. It will attract buyers looking for elevated genre, not broad four-quadrant play.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The premise lands fast: Francis is the attacker, the police are closing in, and the story is building toward Halloween. The script makes that clear through the nightclub assaults, the news reports, and the final gymnasium showdown.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Francis is vivid, contradictory, and playable as both menace and charisma, while Charlie and Diane add strong counterweights. The characters are memorable, though the script leans more on behavior and mood than on a fully rounded emotional arc.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The black-and-white/color shifts, fantasy intrusions, and half-painted clown iconography give the script a distinct authorial stamp. The choice to center a female aggressor who humiliates before attacking is unusually specific and hard to mistake for generic genre writing.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The story has a strong forward pull through repeated attacks, police pressure, and the Halloween endpoint, but it moves in episodic bursts rather than a tightly escalating chain. Several domestic and dreamlike passages deepen texture more than propulsion.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The script’s core idea is fresh in a way that is easy to explain: a charismatic teacher/assailant whose violence is tied to humiliation and performance. It’s memorable, though the surrounding domestic material is more familiar than the central conceit.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The school, the police station, the nightclub circuit, and the two households create a specific social ecosystem with recurring pressure points. The world feels lived-in, especially through the class dynamics, marriage tensions, and the citywide rumor mill.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The script has a very particular register: grotesque, lyrical, funny, and unsettling all at once. Francis’s banter, the fantasy cutaways, and the abrupt violence create a tonal identity that is difficult to imitate.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: There are clear seeds of deeper material around shame, performance, motherhood, and inherited damage, especially in the Diane/Charlie flashback and Francis’s split self-image. The script suggests more beneath the surface than it fully cashes in on within this feature.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: Francis/Edgar, Francis/Charlie, Diane/Charlie, and Diane/Albert all generate distinct energy, and the dinner-party and car scenes show how easily the relationships produce conflict. This is a strong relationship engine, not just a solo showcase.

lead_characters.name: Francis Cow
lead_characters.demographics: Black woman, 30s, married, high-school English teacher, physically imposing, queer-coded energy not explicit, psychologically volatile.
lead_characters.hook: Francis is the script’s gravitational center: a beautiful, statuesque teacher with a rebel’s swagger, a bully’s appetite for control, and a private ritual of violence that feels half-performance, half-compulsion. She can be seductive, funny, cruel, and oddly tender in the same breath, and the script keeps her unreadable enough to stay dangerous. Her marriage to Edgar is real, but it’s also a stage on which she manages her masks.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is showcase territory in the vein of Rosamund Pike in Gone Girl or Jodie Comer in Killing Eve — a role that lets an actor toggle charm, menace, erotic charge, and deadpan comedy inside the same scene. The prize here is a signature antiheroine part with iconography, quotable dialogue, and a final-act reveal that resets how the audience sees her.

lead_characters.name: Charlie Bell
lead_characters.demographics: Mixed-race teenage boy, 15, androgynous, emotionally fragile, socially alienated, student.
lead_characters.hook: Charlie is the wounded observer who sees too much and has too little power to stop any of it. He’s drawn to Francis’s volatility and repelled by his mother Diane’s cruelty, which makes him the story’s most vulnerable moral witness. His sleepwalking, bruises, and longing for escape give him a haunted, almost ghostlike presence.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Lucas Hedges in Manchester by the Sea or Timothée Chalamet in Beautiful Boy a chance to play sensitivity under pressure and make fragility feel cinematic. The showcase is emotional transparency: fear, yearning, humiliation, and the slow accumulation of a breaking point.

lead_characters.name: Edgar Cow
lead_characters.demographics: Black man, 30s, husband, detective, emotionally devoted, socially polished.
lead_characters.hook: Edgar is the loving husband who keeps trying to metabolize the impossible: his wife’s cruelty, her secrecy, and the city’s growing suspicion. He’s warm, funny, and observant, but the script also lets him carry shame and denial, which makes him more than a generic spouse. He’s the emotional ballast of the Francis storyline, even when he’s being quietly outmaneuvered.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Sterling K. Brown in This Is Us or Jeffrey Wright in Westworld a chance to play intelligence, restraint, and emotional injury without losing authority. The appeal is the close-up work: a man trying to love someone he cannot fully know.

lead_characters.name: Diane Bell
lead_characters.demographics: White woman, 50s, Charlie’s mother, wealthy, alcoholic, theatrical, emotionally abusive.
lead_characters.hook: Diane is a force of nature built out of vanity, grief, intoxication, and control. She can be comic, monstrous, seductive, and pitiful within a single scene, and the script gives her a vivid, almost operatic volatility. Her relationship to Charlie is the story’s ugliest emotional engine, and the flashback makes her damage feel inherited rather than random.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Patricia Clarkson in Sharp Objects or Julianne Moore in The Hours a chance to play glamour collapsing into self-destruction. The showcase is big, risky behavior with emotional undertow — a part that can steal scenes and still leave a bruise.

lead_characters.name: Albert
lead_characters.demographics: Caribbean man, 60s, butler, emotionally contained, observant, loyal.
lead_characters.hook: Albert is the quiet stabilizer in Diane’s chaos and Charlie’s only consistent adult refuge. He speaks sparingly, but the script uses him as a moral witness and a pressure valve, which gives him unusual dignity for a supporting domestic role. He’s the one character who seems to understand the family’s damage without being consumed by it.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Mahershala Ali in Moonlight or Delroy Lindo in Da 5 Bloods a chance to project authority through stillness. The showcase is controlled presence: the power of a performer who can change the temperature of a room without raising his voice.

lead_characters.name: Lawrence Cloud
lead_characters.demographics: Black man, 40s, detective, Edgar’s partner and friend, grounded, dryly comic.
lead_characters.hook: Lawrence is the procedural anchor and the script’s most natural straight man, but he’s not just there to move plot. His marriage strain with Jill and his friendship with Edgar give him enough personal friction to feel like a real person inside the investigation. He’s the one who helps translate the city’s chaos into a case.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Wendell Pierce in The Wire or Shea Whigham in Boardwalk Empire a chance to be both grounded and scene-stealing. The appeal is authority with comic timing — a detective who can carry exposition without feeling like exposition.

lead_characters.name: Jill Cloud
lead_characters.demographics: Black woman, 40s, Lawrence’s wife, emotionally raw, infertile, socially sharp.
lead_characters.hook: Jill is the script’s most openly wounded adult woman outside Francis, and her resentment gives the dinner scenes real bite. She’s grieving, defensive, and perceptive, which makes her both sympathetic and dangerous in conversation. Her inability to tolerate Francis is rooted in pain, not just dislike.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Regina Hall in Support the Girls or Carrie Coon in The Leftovers a chance to play hurt, intelligence, and social friction at once. The showcase is emotional volatility with a polished surface.

lead_characters.name: Patrick Thiel
lead_characters.demographics: Black man, 40s, science teacher, observant, concerned, slightly peripheral.
lead_characters.hook: Patrick functions as the school’s watchful conscience, noticing Francis before most people do. He’s not central to the plot mechanics, but he gives the school world a credible adult counterpoint and a useful witness to Francis’s instability. His unease helps externalize what others are only beginning to suspect.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a solid character-actor role in the vein of Courtney B. Vance in The People v. O.J. Simpson — a part that gets value from intelligence, restraint, and reaction. The showcase is the slow realization that something is off.

lead_characters.name: Mrs. Newlander
lead_characters.demographics: Black woman, 50s, guidance counselor, stern, no-nonsense.
lead_characters.hook: Mrs. Newlander is the school’s institutional spine, the adult who refuses to indulge Charlie’s evasions. She’s not flashy, but she’s memorable because she speaks in a way that cuts through the script’s more theatrical behavior. She gives the school scenes a hard-edged realism.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives a veteran character actor a clean, memorable lane — think Viola Davis in a supporting authority role before the lead-level spotlight. The showcase is command: a few scenes, maximum control.

lead_characters.name: Freddy
lead_characters.demographics: Teenage girl, 17, pretty, bold, socially agile.
lead_characters.hook: Freddy is the one teenage character who can meet Charlie’s weirdness without collapsing under it. She’s flirtatious, blunt, and self-possessed, which makes her a welcome tonal counterweight to the adults’ damage. She also gives Charlie a brief, believable shot at normal teenage desire.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Kaitlyn Dever in Booksmart or Odessa A’zion in Hellraiser a chance to be sharp, funny, and emotionally legible fast. The showcase is chemistry and attitude in a compact amount of screen time.

lead_characters.name: Danielle Lager
lead_characters.demographics: White woman, 20s, nightclub victim, injured, frightened.
lead_characters.hook: Danielle is one of the victims who helps define Francis’s pattern, and her interview scene is crucial because it gives the attacks a human cost. She’s not a deep character, but she’s an effective witness whose details help the investigation take shape. The painted smile description is one of the script’s cleanest external images.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a strong single-scene showcase for a young actor who can play shock and specificity, similar to the victim roles that anchor true-crime thrillers. The performance opportunity is to make a procedural interview feel lived-in.

lead_characters.name: Sandy Lyle
lead_characters.demographics: Black woman, 50s, Diane’s friend, polished, socially successful.
lead_characters.hook: Sandy is the social mirror Diane resents, and the yacht sequence uses her to expose Diane’s jealousy and shame. She’s not deeply developed, but she’s important as the person onto whom Diane projects old wounds. Her presence helps the flashback and party scenes feel socially specific.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives a seasoned actor a clean social-status part — polished, watchful, and quietly combustible. The showcase is the ability to imply history without speeches.

rights_flags.detail: Carl's Jr. is named on the page and used in a plot beat.
Glen Miller Orchestra is specifically named as source music in the Diane living-room scene.
Wonder Woman is used as a Halloween costume reference for Jill.
Tyler Durden is referenced in Francis's description.
Jack Napier is used as a named cannabis strain reference.
Poe, Joyce, and Edgar Allan Poe are referenced as literary names, but not clearance-sensitive in the same way as branded IP.

platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release model: specialty theatrical or streaming original with festival launch potential

budget.note: Contemporary locations keep the footprint controlled, but the nightclub fights, Halloween dance chaos, yacht party, flashback pool sequence, and repeated night work add scope pressure.

casting.note: Francis is a narrow, high-voltage lead who has to play seduction, menace, comedy, and physical aggression; Charlie also needs a teen actor with unusual sensitivity and edge.

development.note: The script’s strongest asset is its tonal and psychological singularity, but the buyer conversation will focus on how to frame Francis’s violence, how much of the fantasy language to preserve, and how to position the ending without softening the provocation.

comp_set.title: Promising Young Woman
comp_set.why_it_comps: Shares the female-centered revenge/violence lane, the stylized surface, and the sense of a protagonist weaponizing performance.

comp_set.title: Killing Eve
comp_set.why_it_comps: The appeal of a charismatic, dangerous woman whose behavior is as entertaining as it is alarming maps closely to Francis.

comp_set.title: May
comp_set.why_it_comps: The off-kilter psychological volatility, fetishized body language, and lonely outsider energy feel adjacent to Francis’s split self-image.

comp_set.title: Thoroughbreds
comp_set.why_it_comps: The deadpan cruelty, social unease, and polished suburban surfaces hiding violence are a strong tonal neighbor.

comp_set.title: Pearl
comp_set.why_it_comps: The heightened female psychodrama, periodized self-mythology, and violent theatricality make it a useful comp for tone and audience.

audience_target.primary_audience: Adults who like elevated, female-driven genre films with a sharp psychological edge and a memorable antiheroine.
audience_target.demographics: Skews 25-44, slightly female-leaning, college-educated, streamer/festival audience, strong appetite for prestige genre.

budget_tier.note: Contemporary settings and limited principal cast keep it in indie territory, while the fight scenes, Halloween crowd work, yacht sequence, and stylized visual transitions prevent it from feeling micro.

types_of_buyers: streamer originals teams building female-led genre
producer-directors looking for a breakout lead role
lane_fit.detail: This sits naturally in the lane where character psychology, stylized violence, and a strong central performance are the selling points. The script is more artful and stranger than a standard thriller, but still legible enough to market on premise and image.

ip_potential.detail: Standalone feature. Francis is a strong singular character, but the script does not establish a clean sequel or universe vector beyond this one story.

strengths.what_it_means: This gives the project a casting hook that can open doors with actors and buyers who want a role with attitude, danger, and iconography. It is the kind of part that can anchor a director’s calling-card feature and generate immediate conversation around performance.
strengths.evidence: The nightclub assaults, the half-painted clown smile, and the final Halloween confrontation all build a character who is both predator and performance artist.

strengths.what_it_means: A teacher who is also the city’s female nightclub attacker is a clean, high-concept engine that can be pitched in one breath. That clarity helps with buyers, festival programmers, and actors looking for a bold centerpiece role.
strengths.evidence: The news reports, police interviews, and repeated attacks make the central mystery legible almost immediately.

strengths.what_it_means: The script has a voice that can separate it from generic thriller material and give marketing a distinct visual and tonal identity. Buyers chasing elevated genre want something that feels authored, and this page absolutely does.
strengths.evidence: The black-and-white/color shifts, fantasy hallucinations, and Francis’s absurdly specific dialogue create a signature register.

strengths.what_it_means: Francis/Edgar, Francis/Charlie, and Diane/Charlie all create recurring friction that can sustain scenes without relying on plot mechanics alone. That makes the script attractive to actors and directors who want dialogue scenes with tension, not just set pieces.
strengths.evidence: The dinner table blowup, the car rides with Charlie, and the bedroom confrontation with Edgar all play as character pressure-cookers.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The Halloween climax is a clean event hook.
strengths.what_it_means: The calendar endpoint gives the film a built-in release-season identity and a natural marketing image. It also gives the story a visible countdown that helps buyers understand the shape of the feature quickly.
strengths.evidence: Francis explicitly frames Halloween as the night she wants to go out on, and the final gym sequence pays that off.

whats_special.headline: This is a contained, elevated indie thriller with a genuinely ownable lead role and a visual identity that feels built for a trailer. The script’s biggest commercial asset is that it pairs a star-making antiheroine with a clear Halloween countdown and a production footprint that stays in the indie lane rather than exploding into tentpole scope.

items.area: Francis’s psychology stays more emblematic than legible.
items.detail: The script gives her a powerful surface — swagger, cruelty, erotic charge, humiliation — but the deeper engine of why she attacks is still mostly implied through mood and fantasy. That makes her magnetic, but it also means some buyers will see a performance vehicle before they see a fully bankable character arc.

items.area: The violence pattern is repetitive before the finale.
items.detail: Several nightclub and school beats follow the same rhythm: Francis spots a target, humiliates them, attacks, and exits laughing. The repetition is part of the character design, but it also creates a buyer concern about escalation and whether each set piece is adding a new layer or just restating the same impulse.

items.area: The fantasy language may divide buyers.
items.detail: The black-and-white/color switches, mirror-smile blips, harpoon hallucination, and mermaid sequence give the film a strong signature, but they also push it away from straightforward thriller territory. That is a feature for some buyers and a friction point for others who want the premise to play more cleanly as grounded genre.

items.area: Charlie is vivid but structurally secondary.
items.detail: He has strong scenes with Francis and Diane, but the script never fully turns him into an equal engine; he functions more as witness, victim, and pressure point. That keeps the story centered, but it also narrows the emotional breadth of the ensemble and limits the sense of a broader breakout cast.

items.area: The brand and music references need a legal pass.
items.detail: Carl's Jr., Glen Miller Orchestra, Wonder Woman, Tyler Durden, and Jack Napier are all specifically named on the page. None of them are fatal, but they do create clearance and trademark questions that business affairs will want resolved early.

issues.headline: The main friction is that the script’s most compelling element — Francis herself — is also the least psychologically pinned-down, which makes the film feel like a bold performance piece more than a fully demystified thriller. Buyers will also weigh the repeated attack pattern and the stylized fantasy inserts, which are part of the appeal but may narrow the lane to elevated-genre champions rather than broad commercial buyers.
